Chapter 4: Breaking Free from Comparison and Financial Shame
Ever notice how scrolling through social media can make you feel like everyone else is just... crushing it at life? Perfect vacations, brand-new cars, designer outfits—these snapshots flood your feed and suddenly, there’s this quiet pressure to keep up. But here’s the thing: what you’re seeing is rarely the whole story.
Let me tell you about someone who went through this firsthand. Fresh out of college, this guy found himself always measuring his life against his friends’. If one of them got a new car, he’d start feeling embarrassed about his old sedan. When another friend posted photos from a tropical getaway, he couldn’t help but wonder why he wasn’t doing the same. The pressure kept building, until he started swiping his credit card just to try and keep pace—telling himself he deserved those experiences too.
But then, the debt piled up. That’s when he finally stopped to ask himself: Why am I caught in this cycle? He realized the folks he envied probably had their own money worries, just hidden behind those polished photos. When he shifted his focus to his own goals—rather than someone else’s highlight reel—the shame started to fade.
Here’s something to pay attention to: financial shame often sneaks in when we believe our mistakes say something about who we are. Maybe you’ve missed a payment, taken out a loan that snowballed, or worked a job that barely covered the bills. It’s easy to think you’re the only one struggling, but honestly, almost everyone has been there at some point. The real problem? We don’t talk about it, so the shame just grows in silence.
Take the story of a young woman weighed down by student loans. She avoided talking about her debt, worried her friends or family would judge her. Finally, she opened up to a close friend—and was stunned to find out they were in the same boat. That conversation was a relief. It broke the isolation and opened up practical support she never expected.
Now, letting go of comparison and shame isn’t something that happens overnight. But it is possible. It starts by recognizing that everyone’s financial journey is their own—shaped by unique ups and downs. There’s no single path to success, and there’s absolutely no shame in starting over, or asking for help. When you focus on your own values and goals, instead of what you think others expect, you can start building a financial life that’s real, meaningful, and sustainable.
